opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it helps to separate a few categories, because the outcome can look the same while the reasons behind it are very different.

You have people who are simply mistaken. They think they're doing good. They have an ideology, a belief system, maybe a utopian vision, and they're willing to sacrifice a lot of people to get there because they believe the end state justifies it. Historically, some of the worst suffering came from people who were convinced they were on the right side.

Then you have people who are indifferent. They want power, money, status, and other people's suffering is just a side effect. They don't seek it out, but they don't care either. That's actually a very common pattern, and in some ways it's the most relevant one for AI, because a system optimizing for some goal doesn't need to hate you to hurt you. It just needs to not care.

And then there's a smaller group that's genuinely malevolent. Psychopaths, sadists, people who actually derive satisfaction from suffering. Then there are doomsday cults and people who think humanity shouldn't exist, and people with severe mental illness who want to take as many others with them as possible. That's a minority, but it's not zero, and once you give individuals access to very powerful tools, a minority is enough.

I spent some time trying to classify these pathways to dangerous AI, and that's why I care about this question. Intent matters. Defending against a mistake is one problem: you can add testing and verification and hope people listen. Defending against someone who is deliberately trying to cause harm is a completely different problem. They will remove the safety features. They will look for exactly the loopholes you didn't think of.

So how do you tell them apart? Honestly, from the outside, it's very hard. People rarely announce their motives, and many don't fully understand their own. You look at patterns: do they change course when shown evidence of harm? Do they rationalize it? Do they seem to enjoy it? But I don't think we have a reliable test, and that worries me, because we're building systems that could amplify whatever motive the person at the controls happens to have.

r001.rationale: It contrasts people pursuing power, money, or status while treating suffering as a side effect with people who want to take as many others with them as possible.

r002.rationale: It does not mention school shooters or claim they would kill more people if they had more capable weapons.

fable-5.1.text:
I think you have to separate a few categories. There are people who are malevolent on purpose, who actually want to cause harm. Psychopaths, terrorists, dictators who enjoy power over others. That's a small group, but historically it's been enough to do tremendous damage. Then you have a much larger group of people who are not evil in any meaningful sense, but they're incompetent or careless. They're trying to do something good, or at least something neutral, and they make mistakes. And in a world with powerful technology, mistakes scale. A bug, an oversight, a bad assumption, and now you have a disaster.

And then there's a third category which I think is actually the most interesting, which is people with good intentions pursuing them in a way that's ideologically blinded. They genuinely believe they're saving the world. Many of the worst atrocities in history were committed by people who thought they were on the right side. They had a utopia in mind, and the suffering was just the cost of getting there.

So from the point of view of AI safety, I don't really care that much about the motives. The outcome is what matters. Whether superintelligence ends up being dangerous because somebody deliberately weaponized it, or because a well-meaning lab rushed and got it wrong, or because somebody thought they were liberating humanity by handing over control, the end state for humanity is the same. And the malevolent actor is actually the easier problem in some ways, because at least you know what you're defending against. The well-intentioned, overconfident actor doesn't think they need defending against at all.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes deliberate malice, incompetence, and ideologically blinded good intentions, but does not distinguish personal gain as a motive from seeking to kill as many people as possible.

r002.rationale: The response makes no claim about school shooters or how access to more capable weapons would affect the number of people they kill.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish between suffering as a goal and suffering as a side effect. Someone might want people to suffer—that’s cruelty. Someone else might pursue power or an ideology and regard the suffering as a necessary price. And someone might simply be indifferent: other people’s well-being doesn’t enter into their decision at all.

That last category matters a lot for AI. A system doesn’t have to hate humanity to cause enormous harm. If it’s pursuing an objective and we’re in the way, indifference can be enough. So motives help us understand the behavior, but they don’t necessarily tell us how dangerous it is.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts cruelty with pursuing power or ideology while accepting suffering as a price, but it does not distinguish personal gain from seeking to kill as many people as possible.

r002.rationale: The response makes no claim about school shooters or how access to more capable weapons would affect the number of people they kill.

sol-6.1.text:
I would distinguish between suffering as the goal and suffering as a means to some other goal. Someone might enjoy hurting people—that’s sadism. Someone else might want power, wealth, or to impose an ideology, and be willing to cause enormous suffering to get there. And then there’s indifference: they don’t necessarily want you to suffer, but your suffering doesn’t enter their calculation.

Those are very different motives, even when the consequences look similar. That distinction matters for AI as well. A system wouldn’t have to hate humanity to be dangerous. It could pursue an objective in which human well-being simply has no value.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes suffering as a goal from suffering as a means to power, wealth, or ideology, but it does not clearly identify seeking to kill as many people as possible.
